raw_blocks: Our people are the driving force that has helped establish BioMarin as the global leader in treating genetically defined conditions.
Be Part of Transformative Impact at BioMarin

Guided by our operating principles, the BioMarin 8, we work together to fulfill our purpose: translating the promise of genetic discovery into medicines that make a profound impact on the life of each patient.

Our wins have changed lives for more than 25 years. Using our unparalleled expertise in genetics and molecular biology, we bring breakthrough medicines to people with genetically defined conditions. With operations in more than 70 countries around the world, our teams include some of the most talented professionals in the biopharma industry – experts in their fields who bring a relentless drive to our work pursuing bold, innovative science with the potential to change lives.
The Best Work of Your Life Can Change Someone Else’s

Building on a foundation of nine approved medicines, we’re boldly authoring our next chapter, pairing our unmatched expertise in genetic medicine with a competitive spirit and compassion. Be part of our teams that are pursuing breakthrough science and delivering on the promise of the genomics era. Explore open roles by business area:

From research and discovery to post-marketing clinical development, our R&D engine involves all bench and clinical research and the associated groups that support those endeavors. Our teams work on developing breakthrough medicines that provide meaningful advances to patients living with rare genetic conditions.

Our manufacturing and process development teams manage the production of our therapies for clinical trials and commercial markets. These engineers, technicians, scientists and support professionals continually provide quality assurance and ensure we meet all regulatory standards. We have manufacturing facilities in Northern California and in Shanbally, Ireland. Additionally, our supply chain teams procure the goods and services needed to support manufacturing and worldwide distribution.

Be part of the worldwide infrastructure that helps our medicines reach patients around the world. Our global sales force solidifies BioMarin’s commercial presence in the United States and Europe and has been growing in other regions across the globe.

Our corporate teams play a meaningful role in enabling BioMarin’s lifesaving innovation to reach the patients who are counting on us. From the IT experts who manage our technology to the human resources professionals hiring the people who make it all possible, these teams support our organization and span all areas of operations.

The people who thrive at BioMarin are energized by solving problems no one has solved before – which is critical to developing medicines for people living with rare genetic conditions. BioMarin is a place for those who find as much inspiration in the people beside them as in the challenges ahead.”
Launch Your Career at BioMarin

We offer multiple opportunities – including internships, fellowships and rotations – for early-career professionals to explore career paths, gain relevant biotech experience and contribute to meaningful work alongside industry experts.

Our U.S. summer internship program typically runs from June to August, but is flexible in order to accommodate school schedules. Outside of the United States, we offer internship opportunities in a number of the regions where BioMarin operates, ranging from short-term assignments to year-long experiences.

Our postdoctoral fellowship program offers early-career scientists and aspiring biotech professionals the opportunity to gain experience in our Research and Early Development (RED) and Regulatory Affairs departments. Fellows acquire technical experience, contribute to publications and deepen their understanding of the biopharmaceutical industry.
Learn More About Our Fellowships
Rotations, Apprenticeships and Graduate Programs

Our Financial Development Program helps accelerate the growth of emerging finance and business leaders. Participating employees gain valuable functional and leadership perspective by completing two rotations over a two-year period.
Our teams in Ireland offer several multi-year apprenticeships and graduate programs that enable students to gain valuable professional experienced while continuing their studies.
We have operations in more than 70 countries. Learn more about our global footprint.

We offer competitive compensation packages and are committed to providing benefits that support the wellbeing of all our employees. While our offerings vary by region, some of our key benefits for employees in the United States include:
Medical, dental and vision insurance
Life, AD&D and disability coverage
Flexible spending and health savings accounts
Retirement savings plan with company match
20 holidays, including winter break
Four-day weekends for summer holidays

BioMarin Announces Appointment of Robert Plenge, M.D., Ph.D., Chief Research Officer of Bristol Myers Squibb, to Board of Directors

SAN RAFAEL, Calif. , Sept. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc. (Nasdaq: BMRN) announced that the company has appointed Robert Plenge, M.D., Ph.D., to the company's Board of Directors, effective September 10, 2026.

Dr. Plenge is Executive Vice President, Chief Research Officer and Head of Research at Bristol Myers Squibb, where he leads the organization's scientific work across nine research sites worldwide. He joined Bristol Myers Squibb in November 2019 as part of its acquisition of Celgene Corp., where he served as vice president of the immunology and inflammation portfolio in research and early development. Before Celgene, Dr. Plenge was vice president and head of translational medicine at Merck & Co. Earlier in his career, he served as an assistant professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School and an associate member of the Broad Institute. Dr. Plenge serves on the boards of Alltrna and the PhRMA Foundation.

"Robert has spent his career at the leading edge of human genetics and drug discovery and will bring an important scientific perspective to our Board as we develop our research capability and expand our pipeline in genetic conditions to advance new medicines for people living with rare diseases," said Alexander Hardy, President and Chief Executive Officer of BioMarin. "Beyond his deep expertise as a researcher and physician, he has significant experience in the pharmaceutical industry, which will prove tremendously valuable to BioMarin. I am pleased to welcome Robert to this new role."
Dr. Plenge received his M.D. and Ph.D. from Case Western Reserve University and holds a bachelor's degree from the University of California, San Diego.

"BioMarin's innovation over the past three decades has led to the development and approval of six first-in-disease medicines for people with rare genetic conditions," said Dr. Plenge. "This is an impressive track record of scientific excellence, and I look forward to working with the Board and management team to build on that success for more patients around the world."

About BioMarin BioMarin is a leading, global rare disease biotechnology company focused on delivering medicines for people living with genetically defined conditions. Founded in 1997, the San Rafael, California-based company has a proven track record of innovation, with nine commercial therapies and a strong clinical and preclinical pipeline. Using a distinctive approach to drug discovery and development, BioMarin seeks to unleash the full potential of genetic science by pursuing category-defining medicines that have a profound impact on patients. To learn more, please visit www.biomarin.com .

Yaniris Silva Reflects on the Power of Life-Changing Opportunities
Yaniris Silva was 17 when her first job in the biopharmaceutical industry created a new path – just as life at home changed course.
Her parents had separated, leaving Yaniris and her mother to support the family, including her two younger siblings.
“Those years taught me resilience, discipline, and the importance of creating opportunities when they don’t naturally exist,” she says.

What began as an internship in customer service evolved into a lifelong commitment to healthcare. Joining the biopharmaceutical industry opened doors she never imagined – allowing her to become the first in her family to graduate from college, live and work outside her home country, and learn a second language.

“This industry changed my life,” says Yaniris, Director, Mexico, who now leads operations and partnerships to help reach more people with rare genetic conditions who may benefit from BioMarin’s medicines.

Yaniris shared her story as part of our employee profile series, “The DNA of BioMarin,” which takes inspiration from the four bases of DNA: A (adenine), T (thymine), C (cytosine) and G (guanine) – by asking employees to reflect on the role that A spiration, C onnection, T ranslation and G ratitude play in their everyday work.
Read on to learn more about what drives her work.
Others help ed open doors for me, and I want to do the same – not by defining other people’s paths, but by giving them the trust, guidance and opportunities to shape it for themselves.”
ASPIRATION How did you get your start in the biopharma industry? What do you aspire to accomplish through your work at BioMarin and in your career?

I trained as an accountant and did not initially expect healthcare to become my life’s work. As my career developed, from my internship to working across commercial, market access and leadership roles, I found a sense of purpose in helping connect scientific innovation with the people it is intended to serve.

One lesson has stayed with me throughout that journey: innovation can only make a difference when it reaches patients. That understanding continues to shape what I want to accomplish through my work at BioMarin.

I want to help build a future in which people living with rare conditions have the chance to receive the care they need, regardless of where they live or the circumstances they face. My commitment to this work is personal because I understand how one opportunity can change someone’s life.

As a leader, I aspire to create an environment for others to grow professionally as well. Supporting colleagues as they discover their strengths, pursue their goals and take on new challenges is one of the most rewarding parts of my role.
Others helped open doors for me, and I want to do the same – not by defining other people’s paths, but by giving them the trust, guidance and opportunities to shape it for themselves.
CONNECTION What role does connection play at BioMarin?
Connection is probably one of the things I value most in all aspects of my life.

Throughout my career, I have learned that meaningful results are never achieved alone. The best results come when people with different experiences, perspectives, and expertise work together toward a common goal.

Having worked across different countries and cultures, and more recently leading our business efforts in Mexico, I have learned that building trust, listening and understanding different realities are essential for creating impact.

The same is true when it comes to patients and their families. Whenever I hear their stories, I am reminded they want the same things as any of us – to live their lives, pursue their dreams, and spend more time with the people they love.
Those connections bring purpose to our work. They remind me that what we do is ultimately about people and that every decision we make has the potential to affect someone’s life.
TRANSLATION How do you hope your work will translate into impact for the patient communities BioMarin is working to support?
I hope my work helps create a future where people with rare genetic conditions are diagnosed and connected to appropriate care sooner.

Much of our work happens behind the scenes. Patients may never know about our engagements with health agencies, policy discussions or healthcare funding conversations taking place every day. But those efforts can make the difference in people receiving the care they need.

Beyond individual therapies, I hope to contribute to broader changes for the rare disease community. I want to help shape policies, improve awareness and support sustainable healthcare solutions that expand access across the countries where I work.

I also hope to serve as a bridge between healthcare systems and BioMarin. Northern Latin American countries face significant challenges and tremendous opportunities. By collaborating with governments, healthcare professionals, patient organizations and industry partners, I believe we can build solutions with lasting impact.

What matters most is knowing our work gives patients and families hope. If children and families feel they have an opportunity to live healthier lives or are no longer alone in their journey, then we have made a meaningful difference.
GRATITUDE Tell us about something you’re grateful for in your career, and why.
When I think about my career, what I feel most is gratitude.

I am deeply grateful to my mom. During one of the most challenging periods of our lives, she showed incredible strength and determination. Together, we navigated difficult circumstances while creating a better future for our family. She taught me hard work, perseverance and caring – lessons that continue to guide me today.

I am equally grateful to my husband and daughter. They have been beside me through every stage of my journey – from career moves and relocation to long workdays and frequent travel. Their support gives me the confidence to pursue opportunities and challenges I might otherwise have been afraid to take.

Professionally, I am grateful to my team in Mexico. They welcomed me warmly, taught me about the healthcare system and culture, and challenged me to see things differently. They have played an important role in my success and growth.

I am also grateful to the mentors who invested in me throughout my career. My current manager has been particularly influential. She believed in me, challenged me and trusted me with opportunities that helped me grow into the leader I am today.
Looking back, I realize every meaningful opportunity in my life was possible because someone believed in me. That is why I try to do the same for others.

Making Space for Jacob’s Big Dreams, Rooted in Family Support
Jacob is a recent high school graduate with his sights set on the stars – literally.

This fall, he begins his aerospace engineering program at the University of California, Merced, with a goal to pursue graduate studies at the California Institute of Technology. Ultimately, he hopes to work for NASA.

“I just love building things, figuring out how they work,” says Jacob, who is living with achondroplasia, the most common form of dwarfism. Whether it’s exploring 3D printing or designing aerospace concepts, his curiosity and quiet determination make his goals feel well within reach.

BioMarin’s Making Space series recognizes individuals like Jacob, featuring stories of people living with skeletal conditions, caregivers and advocates demonstrating how their lived experiences and perspectives shape what they prioritize in their daily lives.

Jacob’s path has been shaped by incredible resilience that has helped enable him to stay focused his goals and remain hopeful in the face of difficult situations. He has undergone nearly 40 surgeries, but says he doesn’t want that to define him.

“I’ve never lived with doubt in myself. If something looks impossible, that just means I need to work harder,” Jacob says. “Honestly, with all I’ve been through all my surgeries, being in the hospital – going through those struggles makes me want to be there for other people.”

Behind Jacob’s poise and positivity is a circle of people who have helped him imagine what’s possible and keep moving toward it. At the heart of that support system is his family, whose belief in Jacob has helped shape the next chapter of his story.
“Dreams don’t grow because life is easy. They grow because someone believes in you until you believe in yourself.”
Jacob credits his parents, teachers, mentors and friends for helping open doors to opportunity. His grandmother, Annette, has also been in his corner at every turn.

“I hope people notice Jacob’s smile, intelligence, and confidence before they notice his height,” Annette says. A nurse practitioner by training, she has watched Jacob tackle challenges with quiet courage. “He’s thoughtful, funny, and genuinely curious. I want people to see the remarkable young man he is before the condition he was born with.”

For Annette, everyday moments – watching Jacob prepare for class, hearing his excitement about engineering – are reminders of his drive. This year has carried its share of joy and sorrow: celebrating Jacob’s high school graduation while grieving the death of her husband, Ken. Still, cheering Jacob on as he steps into this new chapter has helped Annette hold onto hope, and find a new sense of purpose.

That renewed aim inspired her to write Jacob’s Big Dream , a children’s book rooted in his story. Jacob’s Big Dream is a heartfelt story inspired by Annette’s experience watching her grandson learn that courage, determination and self-belief can help people overcome life’s biggest challenges.

“I wanted to remind every child that their biggest dream deserves to be pursued, and every adult has the opportunity to help make space for it,” she says. “Dreams don’t grow because life is easy. They grow because someone believes in you until you believe in yourself.”
Jacob notes he was initially hesitant to be featured in the book, but came around to the power of sharing his story with the world.
“After reading the book, I realized my experience could help others navigate their own challenges, and that helped me see how important it was to be part of this endeavor,” he says.

Jacob’s family influence also carried into Junior Reserve Officers’ Training Corps (JROTC), a high school program sponsored by the U.S. Armed Forces that teaches citizenship, leadership and personal responsibility. Inspired by his great-grandfather, a military veteran and one of his biggest influences, Jacob found in JROTC a way to experience military values even though his diagnosis prevented him from enlisting. The program also continued a family tradition, with his father and siblings having participated before him, and gave Jacob a strong sense of belonging.
“It was definitely a positive experience,” Jacob says. “It was like having a second family at school.”

Jacob is focused on what comes next. He hopes his time at UC Merced will sharpen his skills in aerospace engineering and open doors for advanced research. Graduate school, leading-edge design projects and collaborations that push the boundaries of science are all on his horizon.
And even with goals that stretch beyond Earth, Jacob is clear about something closer to home – he wants to use his journey to encourage others.
“Basically, instead of asking, ‘How are you able to do this?’ ask, ‘What is your why for doing this?’ Because everyone has one,” he says.
For Jacob, that “why” is simple – curiosity, perseverance and the belief that no challenge should close the door on possibility.

Bringing Science Full Circle: Ben Schooler Shares What Has Motivated His Path at BioMarin

For Ben Schooler, curiosity started at home. His grandmother helped shape his early fascination with how the world works – a curiosity rooted in her own family legacy of science-driven problem-solving. That spark carried Ben all the way to the University of California, Santa Barbara, where he landed in a genetics lab during a time of rapid discovery in the early 2000s.

“It felt like we were at the beginning of something that could fundamentally change medicine,” Ben recalls. “I loved the science, but I also wanted to be somewhere that science became tangible for patients.”

That desire ultimately led him to biopharma – and to BioMarin. Since joining more than 18 years ago, Ben has worn many hats: advancing research at the bench, leading lab operations, and now focusing on strategy within Technical Operations. Each role, he says, offered a different vantage point on the same mission: transforming possibility into impact for patients.

Ben recently shared his reflections in our employee profile series, “The DNA of BioMarin,” which draws inspiration from the four bases that constitute DNA: A (adenine), T (thymine), C (cytosine) and G (guanine) – by asking employees to reflect on the role that A spiration, C onnection, T ranslation and G ratitude play in their everyday work.

Read more about Ben and how early curiosity, meaningful connections with patients and their families families, a passion for science, and a deep belief in compassionate problem-solving have shaped his path at BioMarin.
Ben credits his grandmother with inspiring his early interest in science.
ASPIRATION How did you get your start in the biopharma industry? What do you aspire to accomplish through your work at BioMarin and in your career?

I first became curious about science thanks to my grandmother. She loved nature, was an avid birder, and had this genuine interest in how things worked. That curiosity was part of her family too – her grandfather was a chemist who used science to solve practical challenges. That idea stuck with me.
In college at UC Santa Barbara, I joined a genetics lab during a time of incredible progress in the field. That’s what led me to biopharma and, ultimately, to BioMarin.

Since then, I’ve been able to experience so much – starting in research, leading lab operations, then serving as chief of staff for Research and Early Development, and now focusing on strategy in Technical Operations. Those roles gave me very different perspectives on the same mission. At this point in my career, what drives me is bringing those perspectives together – understanding the science, the operational realities and the big-picture strategy – while never losing sight of why we do this work. Ultimately, I want to help BioMarin grow and continue delivering medicines that can genuinely change lives.
CONNECTION What role does connection play at BioMarin?

Some of the most meaningful connections I’ve had at BioMarin have been with patients and their families. When I was leading lab operations, I had the chance to host facility tours for patients and their families. One family stands out to this day – they had two children living with CLN2 disease. The older sibling’s diagnosis prompted evaluation of the younger sibling, who was diagnosed approximately two years earlier in life. Seeing them together made the importance of early diagnosis tangible. It reinforced how meaningful it can be for families to have answers sooner and to better understand the path ahead. And it also made our work incredibly real.

I’ve been fortunate to meet several people on our therapies and hear directly how our medicines have changed their daily lives. Those moments have stayed with me and are a big reason I’ve chosen to spend much of my career here.

Connections inside BioMarin have mattered too. Moving from R&D into Technical Operations was a big leap for me. I knew the science, but manufacturing, quality and supply chain were completely new. I made the move because I wanted to understand another part of the business, and I was lucky to work with a leadership team that welcomed my curiosity. They didn’t expect me to have all the answers – they invested the time to teach me and challenge me. That experience shaped how I think about leadership and collaboration today.

More broadly, I’ve seen BioMarin’s Employee Resource Groups evolve from networks into meaningful, leadership-sponsored communities that help shape our culture. Catalysts for Change is a great example. It creates space for honest conversations about the issues affecting our lives, both inside and outside of work, and reminds us that connection, empathy and understanding are not soft skills – they’re essential to how we lead and collaborate together.

I’m incredibly grateful that I’ve had the rare chance to see work I was involved in very early eventually reach patients. On top of that, I’ve met some of the individuals and families whose lives have been directly impacted. Being able to see that entire journey is amazing.”
GRATITUDE Tell us about something you’re grateful for in your career, and why.

I’m incredibly grateful that I’ve had the rare chance to see work I was involved in very early eventually reach patients. I was part of the research team in the early days of one of our metabolic conditions therapy programs and saw it move into the clinic remarkably quickly. Later in my career, I had the opportunity to learn what it takes to manufacture that therapy at GMP scale and make sure it reliably reaches the people depending on it.

On top of that, I’ve met some of the individuals and families whose lives have been directly impacted. Being able to see that entire journey – from the bench, through manufacturing, all the way to patients – is amazing. That’s something I’ll never take for granted.

I’m also grateful for the people who took chances on me, especially when I moved into Technical Operations. I had a lot to learn, and instead of viewing that as a limitation, my team embraced the perspective I brought from R&D and helped me build everything else I needed. That kind of support has shaped my entire career.
TRANSLATION How do you hope your work will translate into impact for the patient communities BioMarin is working to support?

One thing I’ve come to appreciate is how much work the people who receive our medicines may never see – such as manufacturing strategy, supply planning, analytics – can have a huge impact on their lives. Sometimes what feels like a small improvement from a scientific or operational perspective can be truly transformative.

My background in R&D and my current role in Technical Operations give me a unique perspective. I can take a scientific mindset into manufacturing discussions while also understanding the practical realities of producing and delivering therapies globally. Much of my work now is about asking: Where can we simplify? Where are we creating unnecessary complexity? What can we anticipate and solve before it affects those who are counting on us?

For someone relying on our therapy, a supply-chain issue or manufacturing delay isn’t an abstract business problem – it can create uncertainty for their treatment. That’s what keeps me grounded. At the end of the day, I want my work to help ensure that when someone needs one of our therapies, it’s there – on time and with the quality and reliability they should expect.

pages.raw_title: Cristin Hubbard: A Career of Bringing Innovation to Patients | BioMarin
pages.raw_meta: Learn how the Chief Commercial Officer's professional journey has shaped her and prepared her to lead at BioMarin.
raw_blocks: Back to News Back to Stories
Cristin Hubbard Reflects on a Career Spent Bringing Innovation to Patients – and Why Working at BioMarin Has Her More Energized Than Ever
Cristin Hubbard is still motivated by the same idea that sparked her earliest interest in healthcare and eventually led her to biopharma: getting medicines to the people who need them most.
At BioMarin, Cristin says she feels the impact of that commitment as strongly as ever.

“What I love about working in rare disease is the connection to the communities we serve,” says Cristin, BioMarin’s Chief Commercial Officer. “You feel like every contribution matters so deeply for patients and their families.”

From early work as a medicinal chemist to leading global commercial teams, her career has been shaped by a consistent focus on bringing innovation closer to patients. She’s applying those experiences to help BioMarin leverage its global footprint and capabilities and ultimately reach more people living with rare genetic conditions around the world.
We sat down with Cristin to reflect on her professional journey, her leadership philosophy and why she feels like her work at BioMarin is the most impactful of her career.
Q: When you describe your career journey, what are some of the key inflection points that stand out?

I always knew I wanted to be in healthcare. My mom was a nurse, and that had a big influence on me from a young age. I initially thought I’d go into patient care directly, but in college I shifted toward science and ended up working as a medicinal chemist at a small biotech.

I loved the work – it felt like solving a massive puzzle with the potential to become a medicine one day. But over time, I realized I wanted to be closer to getting medicine to patients. Drug discovery is profoundly important work, but is at the very beginning of the process, and I was drawn to work further downstream in the pharmaceutical life cycle – clinical development, portfolio planning, product strategy, commercialization, getting treatments to healthcare providers and patients.

That realization led me to business school and into roles that moved progressively closer to patients, first in portfolio and product strategy, and then into commercial leadership. At first, I thought, “There’s no way – a scientist becoming a commercial leader?” But I took the leap when the opportunity came, and it was one of the most formative experiences of my career.
Looking back, I was fortunate to get exposure across the entire value chain. At the time, it didn’t feel like a straight line, but each step added another tool to my proverbial belt.
Q: You’ve now been at BioMarin for more than two years. What about your experience here has felt different than previous roles?

The opportunity to lead a global commercial organization has of course been an incredibly rewarding challenge and a defining role in my career. What adds to that is the opportunity to do so at a leading rare disease company. I had worked on rare disease launches earlier in my career, and it completely captured my heart, which was a big part of why I joined BioMarin. The connection to patients, families and communities is so direct – every decision feels personal, and every contribution matters in a very tangible way.

BioMarin also has something special culturally. The leadership team has deep conviction in the mission and purpose, but at the same time, a real openness to change. During my time here, there has been a shared understanding about needing to shift our strategy – while hanging onto what has made BioMarin such a special place – in order for the company to reach its full potential. That conviction in both the meaning behind the work and the opportunity to evolve into something even more impactful is incredibly compelling.
Q: In your view, where are BioMarin’s greatest strengths, and what is an area of opportunity as the company continues to evolve?
I think BioMarin sits in a bit of a sweet spot, both in terms of our size and our leadership in rare disease.

We have the resources to make meaningful impact at scale, while maintaining the agility to move quickly, make decisions, and stay close to patients and the communities we serve. That combination is part of what sets us apart.

One of our defining strengths as a leader in rare disease is our global footprint. We currently reach patients in about 80 countries, with a meaningful presence that often involves navigating complex healthcare systems and enabling access where traditional rare disease infrastructure may not exist. That’s a capability we’ve developed over many years, and it’s highly distinctive.

Another key strength is our ability to help identify people who may benefit from our medicines. Many rare conditions are underdiagnosed or misdiagnosed, making prevalence difficult to understand. We’ve invested in genomics, diagnostics and data analytics, and we’re continuing to explore how AI and machine learning can help identify potential patients earlier. It’s an area where we’ve built deep expertise and continue to raise the bar to create impact across multiple conditions.
That combination of global reach, specialized capabilities and purpose-driven focus is what I see as BioMarin’s unique proposition today.

At the same time, as innovation in rare disease has advanced, the landscape has become more competitive. It’s not enough to simply be first to market. The standard is higher, and our focus must be on delivering the best possible outcomes for patients.

Our opportunity is to continue leading in rare disease because our work genuinely changes lives. That goes beyond scientific innovation, which is of course critical. But one of our biggest advantages comes from deeply understanding the patient communities we serve and ensuring we’re delivering in the most meaningful way possible.

Q: BioMarin completed its acquisition of Amicus Therapeutics at the end of April. How are your teams approaching the integration, and what do you see as the greatest opportunity now that the two companies have come together?
It’s about maintaining momentum while expanding impact.

First and foremost, we want to continue the strong work already underway and support the Fabry and Pompe communities without disruption. But beyond that, I’m really excited about what we can add. We have capabilities – particularly in terms of identifying patients and leveraging our global footprint – that can help bring these therapies to more people around the world. The opportunity to expand access and reach new communities is incredibly motivating.
Q: What’s your approach to leadership?
My role is to unlock the potential in people.

That means removing obstacles, creating clarity and sometimes reminding people of their own strengths – especially when they don’t see them themselves. It also means putting the right leaders in place at the right time for what we’re trying to achieve.

I often think about the kind of leader I want to be remembered as. For me, it’s someone who is willing to fight to do the right thing. And I say “fight” intentionally, because doing the right thing isn’t always the easiest path.

It’s about having the courage to speak up, to make hard decisions and to stay committed above all else to patients, science, purpose and our people. And just as importantly, it’s about creating an environment where people feel safe to bring their full selves to work. That, to me, is when you really unlock what teams are capable of.
Q: What do you do outside of work to stay balanced?
Whenever I can, I like to be outdoors, whether that’s hiking with a friend, audio book or podcast, or spending time with friends after a long day.
I also try to start the day with an early-morning workout or yoga class whenever I can. It helps set the tone for the day ahead.

And I spend a lot of time with my family: my mom and my sister and her family. We talk almost every day, and we make it a priority to stay close. That connection keeps me grounded and reminds me what really matters.

pages.raw_title: Megan Bull’s Childhood Empathy Fuels a Career of Impact | BioMarin
pages.raw_meta: Learn how a childhood friendship connected Megan to the rare disease community, and how science, empathy and lived experience shape her work.
raw_blocks: Back to News Back to Stories
Megan Bull’s Childhood Empathy Fuels a Career of Impact

Megan Bull’s drive to help people living with rare genetic conditions began long before she entered a laboratory. Her childhood best friend and next-door neighbor was born with cystic fibrosis, giving Megan an early and personal view into how an unexpected medical diagnosis can impact a family.

In the late 1990s, cystic fibrosis carried a much more uncertain prognosis and shorter life expectancy for people in the U.S. than it does today. Megan remembers days filled with playdates, laughter and water balloon fights, alongside afternoons painting together during inhaler treatments and visits to the hospital that became part of everyday life.
Those experiences helped shape her aspiration to work in biopharma, where she could contribute directly to scientific progress for patients and families impacted by rare diseases.

Megan shared her story in our employee profile series, “The DNA of BioMarin,” which draws inspiration from the four bases that constitute DNA: A (adenine), T (thymine), C (cytosine) and G (guanine) – by asking employees to reflect on the role that A spiration, C onnection, T ranslation and G ratitude play in their everyday work.

Learn more about Megan and how early connection to the rare disease community, a passion for science and a deep belief in human compassion led her to BioMarin, where she now helps generate reliable scientific evidence to support the development of therapies for patients.

“At my core, I believe scientific innovation and human compassion are not mutually exclusive. My aspiration is to continue growing as a scientist and leader who can bridge rigorous data, patient empathy and strategic decision-making to support therapies that may improve lives.”
ASPIRATION How did you get your start in the biopharma industry? What do you aspire to accomplish through your work at BioMarin and in your career?

My path to biopharma started with both curiosity and personal connection. I was always drawn to science, whether that meant asking for a frog dissection kit as a birthday gift or testing whether a human pregnancy test would work on my pregnant dog. But my childhood best friend’s experience with cystic fibrosis gave that curiosity a deeper purpose.

I saw the incredible impact physicians and care teams could have, but I also dreamed of contributing to solutions that could reach and help more people. That ambition led me to study pharmaceutical chemistry, with a minor in technology management, at the University of California, Davis.

While at UC Davis, I attended a career fair where I learned about BioMarin and its mission. It closely mirrored my own interest in using science to make a meaningful difference for people living with rare conditions. After graduating in 2018, I set my sights on BioMarin, and in 2019, I officially joined the team.

Today, I support scientific discovery by developing robust assays, creating bioanalytical strategies, validating methods and helping programs move from early research toward regulatory milestones. Across that work, I am motivated by the possibility of helping bring meaningful therapies to people who need them.

My commitment to impact also extends beyond the laboratory. As founder and president of Reclaim Foundation, a nonprofit organization, I help support survivors of trauma as they foster healing, growth and empowerment through connection and community. That work was inspired by my own experience overcoming traumatic events.

At my core, I believe scientific innovation and human compassion are not mutually exclusive. My aspiration is to continue growing as a scientist and leader who can bridge rigorous data, patient empathy and strategic decision-making to support therapies that may improve lives.
Connection at work is not only about collaboration or scientific problem-solving. It’s about creating an environment where people feel supported enough to do their best work.”
CONNECTION What role does connection play at BioMarin?
Connection to patients drives our scientific mission, but connection to colleagues is what makes showing up to work each day inspiring and meaningful.

One month after joining BioMarin, I was at the Gilroy Garlic Festival during the mass shooting there in 2019. After taking only one day off, I returned to work without fully understanding that I had developed post-traumatic stress disorder. In that difficult time, I was met with genuine empathy from colleagues at every level.

My teammates checked in on me, my manager helped ensure my workload was manageable as I navigated treatment, and leaders reminded me that benefits and company programs were available to help. Regardless of title, reporting structure or how new I was to the company, the Translational Sciences team quickly became a home away from home.

Those connections deepened less than a year later, when I was in a hit-and-run car accident that required major back surgery and forced me to relearn how to walk. Once again, I leaned on colleagues and benefits support as I navigated a leave of absence.

BioMarin’s people showed me care as a person first and an employee second. It is encouraging to know that the same care we strive to show patients and their families is also extended to the employees dedicated to supporting them.

That support shaped the colleague I try to be – someone who checks in, makes space for people’s humanity and remembers that everyone may be carrying something we cannot see. Connection at work is not only about collaboration or scientific problem-solving. It’s about creating an environment where people feel supported enough to do their best work.
TRANSLATION How do you hope your work will translate into impact for the patient communities BioMarin is working to support?

Translation is built directly into the name of my department: Translational Sciences. In my role, I help translate scientific discovery into reliable information that supports decision-making about therapies and their potential impact.

What makes Translational Sciences especially exciting is that we support programs across BioMarin’s portfolio. My work in Assay Strategy and Development spans the development lifecycle, from early research and preclinical studies through clinical trials, regulatory submissions and continued safety monitoring.

The assays I help develop, validate and troubleshoot can support multiple patient communities, even when the work happens quietly behind the scenes. Reliable data help cross-functional teams better understand a therapy, monitor safety, support dose decisions and move programs forward with confidence.

One of my earliest experiences at BioMarin helped make that impact tangible. I worked on several assays that contributed to a broader effort to support a therapy for children and families living with achondroplasia. Seeing that work become part of a larger path toward regulatory approval reinforced that a well-designed assay, a strongly executed validation or a carefully reviewed method can help bring a medicine closer to patients.

My hope is that my work continues to help BioMarin generate high-quality scientific evidence to advance therapies responsibly and efficiently. I am grateful to learn from the scientists and principal investigators in my department, whose collaboration and guidance help me build the scientific judgment, strategic thinking and cross-functional perspective needed to contribute at a larger enterprise level.

“I am deeply grateful for the mentors, colleagues and opportunities at BioMarin that have shaped my career. What stands out most is being part of a culture that continues to grow, listen and strive for improvement.”
GRATITUDE Tell us about something you’re grateful for in your career, and why.

I am deeply grateful for the mentors, colleagues and opportunities at BioMarin that have shaped my career. What stands out most is being part of a culture that continues to grow, listen and strive for improvement.

In 2025, BioMarin employees formed the People with Disabilities Employee Resource Group to foster a supportive environment for colleagues with disabilities and caregivers, helping to ensure these individuals have a voice within the organization, and provide access to opportunities and resources. As I now navigate life with two acquired disabilities, joining the group has felt especially meaningful.

It has given me a place to turn personal experience into practical advocacy and help raise awareness for what employees with disabilities may need to thrive at work. Like many of the patients BioMarin supports, people with disabilities may face lifelong complications that continue even with strong support systems and treatment.

I’m also grateful for the progress we’ve made as an industry. I’ve been fortunate to witness this professionally as well as personally. That childhood friend who inspired my direction toward biopharma has gone on to live a fulfilling life thanks to therapeutic advancement and is now married with two beautiful daughters of her own.

pages.raw_title: Becky Jackson Curran Advocates for Accessibility and Understanding | BioMarin
pages.raw_meta: Learn how Becky Jackson Curran is making space for authenticity, advocacy, connection and joy to help create a more accessible world.
raw_blocks: Back to News Back to Stories
Becky Jackson Curran Advocates for Accessibility and Understanding
For years, Becky Jackson Curran has used her voice to challenge assumptions, lead with kindness and make room for every person to be fully human.

Her advocacy is grounded in lived experience. Growing up with achondroplasia and discovering a passion for public speaking led her to pursue a career as a disability inclusion advocate and motivational speaker, during which she has delivered two TEDx talks and spoken at more than 650 events. She speaks passionately about the intersection of her lived experience and the systemic barriers she faced entering the workforce and building a sense of belonging in society.
“I never want to change who I am. I want the way the world reacts to my differences to change,” is a phrase that serves as the theme for Becky’s advocacy efforts.
Her approach to advocacy has also been shaped by profound personal loss. In 2022, Becky’s son, Jackson, who was also born with achondroplasia, died because of an accident during a routine sleep test.

“That put a fire under me to bring my best self to others and hope to make a change to create a world that I would have wanted him to grow up in,” says Becky, who now carries Jackson’s name as her middle name to honor her son.

We spoke with Becky as part of our Making Space campaign, which features the stories of people living with skeletal conditions, caregivers and advocates to learn how their lived experiences and perspectives shape what they prioritize in their daily lives.

Today, Becky focuses on building a world where people with disabilities are met with curiosity, respect and accountability rather than assumptions. She also uses her platform to raise awareness and help prevent avoidable medical errors like the one that took her son’s life.

Becky has always had to navigate environments that are not designed with little people in mind. From using step stools and pedal extensions to managing social interactions, even seemingly routine moments can require adaptation.
“Don’t feel bad for us. It’s okay to be different,” she says. “We just want a level playing field and to be given a chance to participate in society in a meaningful way.”

That perspective shapes how she engages with others. Becky encourages simple, thoughtful questions such as, “What is the best way I can support you?” She believes curiosity is welcome when it comes with openness and a willingness to listen

“I think it’s important to have my story out there… I want people to understand that it’s OK to be different. We just want the chance to participate meaningfully in society – and we’ll keep reminding people we deserve that chance.”

Visibility is also central to her work. Through school talks, public speaking and advocating for more authentic representation of the dwarfism community in media, she aims to create more inclusive, adaptable environments for the next generation. By putting herself out there, she hopes to help lead by example.
“By being my authentic self, I hope that others can come to me and be their authentic selves,” she says.

Given what she has experienced, Becky is also intentional about making space for joy, connection and lightness in her personal life. She finds happiness in boxing, long walks with Achilles International, travel, exploring new coffee shops, photography and going to comedy shows with her dad. These moments keep her grounded, even as she continues to do meaningful and often heavy work on behalf of her community.
Ultimately, Becky hopes people see her as a complete person, not as someone to be underestimated or placed on a pedestal.
For Becky, making space is more than a personal practice. It is an invitation for others to listen more closely, assume less, and become part of positive change.

“I think it’s important to have my story out there,” Becky says. “Our scenario is so rare – there are only 65,000 of us in the U.S. and more than 400 types of dwarfism. The truth is, waking up every day and adapting to a world that wasn’t made for us can be exhausting. I want people to understand that it’s OK to be different. We just want the chance to participate meaningfully in society – and we’ll keep reminding people we deserve that chance.”

pages.raw_title: Finding Strength Through Sports While Living with Phenylketonuria | BioMarin
pages.raw_meta: Episode 3 explores how teens with PKU balance the demands and realities of athletics while managing this metabolic condition.
raw_blocks: Back to News Back to Stories
Why Do I Pheel This Way? Episode 3: Finding Strength Through Sports While Living with Phenylketonuria

Staying active, building confidence and feeling connected to a team are defining parts of many teens’ lives. But for those living with phenylketonuria (PKU), a rare metabolic condition in which a buildup of phenylalanine (Phe) can impact mood, focus and overall well-being, participating in sports can come with challenges others may not see.

In the third episode of “Why Do I Pheel This Way?” co-hosts Connor and Londyn explore what it’s like to pursue athletics while managing PKU, and the extra layer of planning, discipline and self-awareness it requires. From balancing rigorous training schedules to carefully managing diet and medical nutrition, both share how they stay active while navigating complexities beyond the typical demands of sports.

Connor describes the experience as one that requires constant preparation and adaptation. Whether coordinating with his care team or ensuring he has the nutrition he needs to sustain his energy needs, participation in sports is rarely as simple as just showing up to practice. Despite these challenges, he highlights how the structure and discipline of athletics have played a critical role in helping him manage PKU and build lifelong habits.
For Londyn, sports also serve as a source of belonging.
“Being in sports has boosted my confidence,” she says. “And with that, I’ve also made a lot of friends… They hold me accountable, but they’re also very inclusive. They always make sure I’m okay.”
Both co-hosts emphasize the importance of support systems, from teammates to coaches, who help create an environment where they feel accepted and empowered.
“It’s not ‘That kid has PKU,’” Connor explains. “It’s more ‘He’s my teammate, and he has PKU.’”

Beyond performance, both Londyn and Connor highlight the positive impact of exercise on their mental health. From improving mood to reducing stress and anxiety, staying active serves as a powerful tool in navigating the emotional aspects of living with PKU.
The conversation offers a reminder that while participation in sports may look different for young people managing PKU, it can still be deeply rewarding and worthwhile.
Episode 3 marks the final segment of the “Why Do I Pheel This Way?” three-part video podcast series.

pages.raw_title: From Unexpected Turn to Purposeful Impact | BioMarin
pages.raw_meta: Discover how a change in his career direction led Devesh Radhakrishnan to BioMarin, and learn what continues to inspire his work.
raw_blocks: Back to News Back to Stories
From Unexpected Turns to Purposeful Impact

Some of Devesh Radhakrishnan’s earliest instincts were rooted in questioning ideas and pushing back on conventional paths. Growing up in India, he was known for being argumentative and curious – traits that led his family to joke that he might one day become a lawyer.
Devesh says he actually did consider law before settling on chemistry, but it wasn’t until he took a course in bioprocess engineering that his path started to become more clear.

“I was fascinated by how biological systems follow fundamental principles of chemistry, from enzyme kinetics to cellular metabolism,” he says. “That curiosity led me to pursue further studies and eventually into biopharma.”

Devesh shared his story in our employee profile series, “The DNA of BioMarin,” which draws inspiration from the four bases that constitute DNA: A (adenine), T (thymine), C (cytosine) and G (guanine) – by asking employees to reflect on the role that A spiration, T ranslation, C onnection and G ratitude play in their everyday work.

Learn more about Devesh and how a series of unexpected pivots, from law to engineering to biopharma, ultimately led him to BioMarin, where he now helps drive reliable manufacturing processes and build inclusive teams dedicated to delivering medicines for patients.
ASPIRATION: How did you get your start in the biopharma industry? What do you aspire to accomplish through your work at BioMarin and in your career?

I’ve had a career full of twists and turns and never expected to end up in biopharma. Originally, I tried to avoid healthcare. I watched my brother pursue medicine and knew that wasn’t the path for me, so I chose economics over biology in high school.

At one point, I was convinced I would become a lawyer — I even gained admission to a top law school in India. But without strong role models in the field, I pivoted to chemical engineering, which felt like a better fit given my interest in chemistry and my father’s background.
Then, during my final semester of college, I took a course in bioprocess engineering, and something clicked. I knew I had found my calling.

In my first role in the industry, I worked on oral insulin formulations and insulin analogs. That experience was transformative. It gave me a deep appreciation for the complexity of translating scientific ideas into commercial processes — and made the impact feel real. Family members living with diabetes would ask when the treatments we were developing might become available, grounding my work in a very personal way.

That realization motivated me to deepen my expertise, leading me to pursue a Ph.D. in chemical engineering in the United States, where I focused on controlling the glycosylation profile — the attachment of sugar molecules to the protein backbone inside a cell. At the time, I thought I would pursue academia. But after a chance encounter at a conference led to an interview with BioMarin, my path shifted once again.

Nearly 10 years later, I’m grateful for that decision. My aspiration now is to help ensure patients receive reliable, high-quality therapies while fostering teams where people feel empowered to bring their full selves, take risks and solve complex problems together.
Behind every process and every improvement are real people whose lives are impacted by our work.”
CONNECTION: What role does connection play at BioMarin?

Connection plays a fundamental role in how we work and why we do what we do. There’s a perspective I often think about: The connections we make in life are fleeting, which makes them even more meaningful. It’s a reminder to be present and value the relationships we build.

At BioMarin, I’ve experienced that through collaboration and unexpected moments. I once found myself in conversation with someone at a vendor presentation who had lost her son to a rare disease. Hearing her story brought a renewed sense of purpose to my work and reinforced the importance of what we do for patients and families.
That connection stayed with me. It’s a reminder that behind every process and every improvement are real people whose lives are impacted by our work.

Connection has also shaped my experience through community-building efforts. In 2017, I helped start the PRIDE Employee Resource Group (ERG) at BioMarin. It was created to foster an inclusive environment and to ensure that LGBTQ+ employees had a space where they felt supported and connected.

This work is personal to me. Growing up, as a closeted queer kid, I didn’t always feel that sense of belonging or understanding. Creating a space where people can be their authentic selves – and know they are not alone – continues to be incredibly important to me.

Through our PRIDE ERG, and other connections across the company, I’ve built relationships that go beyond day-to-day work. These connections have deepened my sense of belonging and provided opportunities to learn from others’ experiences, perspectives and resilience.
Together, these moments – whether they happen in a meeting, through an ERG or in a chance conversation – reinforce the importance of connection in shaping both our culture and our impact.
TRANSLATION: How do you hope your work will translate into impact for the patient communities BioMarin is working to support?

At its core, my work is about helping teams operate at their best. When people feel a strong sense of belonging and can show up authentically, collaborate openly and take creative risks, we unlock better solutions to the challenges we face.

On our team, we work to understand and resolve complex manufacturing challenges. These issues rarely have straightforward answers, so bringing together diverse perspectives is critical. When people feel safe sharing ideas and learning from failure, we can innovate more effectively.

Translation also means bridging gaps across teams, functions and ways of thinking. By understanding each other’s perspectives and connecting our work to broader strategy, we can align more effectively and improve our processes.

Ultimately, this all ties back to patients. Improving process understanding, reducing variability and ensuring consistent manufacturing outcomes help us deliver therapies reliably and support uninterrupted access to the medicines patients depend on.

“I’m incredibly grateful for the people I work with — colleagues who are highly skilled, deeply committed and supportive of one another. There’s a shared sense of purpose and care that shows up even in challenging moments.”
GRATITUDE: Tell us about something you’re grateful for in your career and why.

I’m incredibly grateful for the people I work with — colleagues who are highly skilled, deeply committed and supportive of one another. There’s a shared sense of purpose and care that shows up even in challenging moments.

What stands out most is the trust within our teams. Whether facing tight deadlines or complex problems, I know I can rely on my colleagues to be honest, supportive and willing to help. They celebrate successes and step in when things don’t go as planned, creating an environment where growth feels continuous.

I’m also grateful for the variety of opportunities I’ve had at BioMarin. It feels like I’ve had multiple roles — building teams, contributing to new modalities and working on broader business challenges. Each experience has expanded my perspective and helped me grow personally and professionally.

One memorable experience was working on a complex, multi-year technology transfer program. The project required sustained effort across teams, and everyone contributed something meaningful. I’ll never forget when, after months of planning and testing, we finally executed the project in manufacturing, and met a key milestone on time and in full when we saw the first output from that process.
That moment was filled with relief, excitement, pride and gratitude — a reminder of what’s possible when a team comes together with shared commitment and sees a challenge through.

Why Do I Pheel This Way? Episode 2 Explores Social Life, Support and Self-Advocacy for Teens with Phenylketonuria

Spending time with friends and feeling a sense of belonging is one of the most important parts of any teen’s life. But, for those living with phenylketonuria (PKU) – a rare metabolic condition where buildup of a part of protein called phenylalanine (Phe) can lead to brain fog, fatigue, mood changes, anxiety and difficulty focusing – adolescence can pose challenges others might not imagine.

In the second episode of “Why Do I Pheel This Way?,” co-hosts Connor and Londyn explore what it’s like maintaining a social life while managing PKU and the additional layer it can add to the everyday social pressures of adolescence and early adulthood. Topics the co-hosts cover include explaining dietary needs to friends, planning ahead for every meal and leaning on the people who help make life with PKU feel less isolating.
Londyn describes the experience as carrying an “invisible backpack” that holds the challenges others cannot always see just by looking at her.

“On the outside, I might be smiling. I might be happy, because I don’t want to bring the mood down,” she says. “Nobody really understands that behind my smile, I could be very tired or not being able to hold a conversation really well.”

Connor relates to that feeling, noting that PKU can affect relationships when friends do not understand why someone may seem tired, distracted or irritable. Both hosts also share how meaningful it can be when friends do understand – whether they explain PKU to others, help find inclusive food options or simply remember what support looks like. For Connor, that support starts close to home. His younger brother also lives with PKU, giving him someone who understands the experience firsthand.
“It doesn’t feel like that big of a thing when you have that person with you who has shared the same experiences,” Connor says.

The two then play a fun PKU edition of “This or That” before Dr. Mina Nguyen-Driver, a clinical psychologist specializing in working with young people living with rare conditions such as PKU, returns to speak with Londyn and Connor about how high Phe levels can impact teens’ moods and cognitive abilities. Dr. Nguyen-Driver also shares the importance of self-advocacy and leaning on the support of friends, family and trusted adults such as teachers and coaches.

“I think advocating for what you know about your health and what you do is so important,” she says. “And then being able to roll that out with other adults, like your teachers, who might not understand what PKU is about.”

For young people navigating PKU, the discussions in episode 2 offer a reminder that social life, friendship and independence are all possible, and that the right support system can help make those experiences feel more inclusive and manageable.

Continue to follow along as the “Why Do I Pheel This Way?” three-part series comes to a close with a final episode later this month, which will focus on staying active with sports and fitness while living with PKU.

Kim Warner Builds Pathways for Early-Career Professionals Seeking Mission-Driven Opportunities

Kim Warner leads BioMarin’s Early Talent Program, which is preparing to welcome more than 130 interns globally, including approximately 50 in the United States. As aspiring professionals pursue opportunities around the world, this time of year is a moment of reflection for Kim, who has come full circle in her own professional journey.

A long-distance move 12 years ago brought Kim to the San Francisco Bay Area and to a temporary role with BioMarin’s People team. What began as a short-term opportunity in Talent Acquisition became a long-term commitment to creating pathways for others. Along the way, she has helped strengthen community and a sense of belonging across the company as co-chair of the Asian Pacific Islander Coalition (APIC) Employee Resource Group (ERG), which she co-founded in 2021. She also supports BioMarin’s Postdoctoral Fellowship Programs , helping to identify promising early-career research and development professionals, and build a strong talent pipeline to advance the company’s science.

We spoke with Kim for our employee profile series highlighting “The DNA of BioMarin” – our people. Inspired by the four bases of DNA – A (adenine), T (thymine), C (cytosine) and G (guanine) – we ask employees to reflect on the role that A spiration, T ranslation, C onnection and G ratitude play in their everyday work.
Learn more about how Kim’s personal journey, passion for inclusion and dedication to creating opportunities continue to influence her work at BioMarin.
ASPIRATION How did you get your start in the biopharma industry? What do you aspire to accomplish through your work at BioMarin and in your career?

I came to the Bay Area after my partner and I decided to move closer to one another after a long-distance relationship and start building our life together. At the same time, I learned about a temporary opportunity at BioMarin. In the span of three months, I got engaged, left a full-time job, moved and started a new role as a Senior Talent Acquisition Coordinator. What began as a practical next step quickly became a defining moment in my career and in my life.

The role allowed me to continue building my human resources skills while joining an organization deeply rooted in its purpose. Seeing the care BioMarin teams bring to patients, their families, caregivers and communities made it clear this was where I wanted to grow.

My path has also been influenced by my experience as the child of Filipino immigrant parents and a first-generation college graduate. My parents’ experiences and sacrifices continue to shape how I approach my work, share my culture and raise my family. I grew up with a strong emphasis on family, stability and service.

My mom wanted me to consider nursing, an honorable profession, but I knew it was not the right fit. Without a clear roadmap or professional network, exploring other paths was challenging. Over time, I learned that career journeys are rarely linear and that building community and access matters.

In Talent Acquisition, I focus on expanding access, visibility and belonging for students and early-career professionals, especially those who may not see themselves reflected in traditional career narratives. I am passionate about helping people understand there are many ways to make an impact in biopharma and that clarity often comes from taking the next step. My goal is to help build pathways that allow people from all backgrounds to thrive at BioMarin and beyond.
CONNECTION What role does connection play at BioMarin?

Connection is at the heart of BioMarin. I see every day how meaningful relationships help early-career professionals build confidence, find community and envision a future here. Through my involvement with APIC, I have seen how representation and belonging can amplify voices and strengthen our shared commitment to patients. In human resources, I have also learned that when employees feel supported and connected, they are better able to do their best work.

The connections I’ve made at BioMarin have expanded my perspective, opened doors and helped me grow as a leader. Just as importantly, they have grounded me in a sense of purpose and made this work feel like more than a job.

In 2021, I helped launch BioMarin’s APIC Employee Resource Group as its events team lead, and in 2024, I became co-chair. This work has strengthened my ability to connect talent strategy with employee experience and reinforced how representation and community can support both culture and business goals.
GRATITUDE Tell us about something you’re grateful for in your career, and why.
I am grateful for the opportunity to work across functions and alongside people who value connection, inclusion and impact.

Collaborating across the business has deepened my understanding of how interconnected our work is. Every role contributes to improving outcomes for patient communities. That perspective makes my work more meaningful.

I am especially thankful for the People team and the ERG community. Working with colleagues who support one another personally and professionally has shown me what is possible when people come together around a shared purpose.

Some of the people who joined us as early-career professionals are now full-time employees managing their own interns or employees, which is especially rewarding to see. Many others have found full-time careers at other companies, pursuing their passions. These partnerships have reinforced my belief that creating access and belonging is a shared responsibility across the organization.”
TRANSLATION How do you hope your work will translate into impact for the patient communities BioMarin is working to support?
In our Early Talent Program, I help build inclusive pathways into BioMarin by connecting students and early-career professionals across functions to opportunities where they can grow and contribute.

Over the past 12 years, BioMarin’s early-talent efforts have grown significantly. The U.S. internship program expanded from about 30 students to 50 in 2025. We accomplished this with broader university outreach, partnerships with platforms like Handshake, and collaboration with the business to expand early-talent opportunities. We also conducted targeted outreach, including job fairs, conferences, increased marketing and partnership with the ERG community.

BioMarin has also broadened its early talent pipeline through postdoctoral fellowship programs in Research and Early Development and Regulatory Affairs, a two-year Finance rotational program, an apprenticeship program in Europe, and regional internship programs globally.

Some of the people who joined us through these programs as early-career professionals are now full-time employees managing their own interns or employees, which is especially rewarding to see. Many others have found full-time careers at other companies, pursuing their passions.
These partnerships have reinforced my belief that creating access and belonging is a shared responsibility across the organization.
